questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The classes available in Australia were so amazing and hands-on.
I chose JCU because of the location close to the rainforest, outback and the Great Barrier Reef. I wanted to go to a smaller town, where you could easily feel at home.
I thought it was a good opportunity to obtain an academic level of english.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
JCU were very helpful in general!
They had a big market day the first week with all the school clubs, which made it easy to access information about how to become socially active at the school.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wrote questions to the tutor that was assigned to us about safety in Townsville and what was going on in the orientation week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: All the practical information was very easily accessible. I was dissapointed in the planned social events during orientation week. I chose to live off campus and there was a clear lack of events, which made it difficult to meet new friends. I would therefore recommend living in one of the dorms for social reasons.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It took me only three days from arriving in Townsville to find accomodation. There are facebook groups easily accessible. You only speak to the landlords when looking at a share house. This was very strange since you didn't know who you were moving in with. The roomates are from my point of view the most important thing about the accommodation.
I asked to meet my roomates before moving in, but it was a very short conversation.
My landlord turned out to be unreliable and at times very rude, which made all of us residents quite uncomfortable. I think that was an unfortunate turn of events since most landlords are friendly and kind. So be careful and listen to your gut - many good share houses are out there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It makes it much harder to meet people in the beginning.
My roomates were both quite introverted and we didn't do much together, but they were very kind and we had lots of interesting cultural conversations about Australia, China, India and Denmark. In many ways I appreciated the quiet, down to earth vibe at the share house.
Lots of stuff happens on campus all the time and Townsville is difficult to get around in, so find accommodation close to campus:)
It was really nice to live close to the river, with a garden in a quiet neighbourhood. My Australian roomate had a lovely dog!
Your roomates might have very different cleaning habits than you do.
As an exchange student you are often adventurous and socially active contrary to many full degree students. Don't expect the same energy level.
It is cheaper that living on campus. I paid $190 per week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would definitely choose to live on campus at BY or maybe rotary if I had to choose again.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You did your best to register for classes before arriving. JCU sent all the information on your JCU email about when to show up for intro day.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: If you had trouble registering for classes you could go to the student center. My friends who did this got everything fixed quite easily.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to register and find classes that didn't overlap. I chose the four subjects I wanted the most. I would recommend waiting to register untill they open the registration online, because then it becomes clearer which timeslots are labs, lectures and so on, so you might not have to attend all timeslots.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The class registration was quite confusing because sometimes you only had to attend some of the timeslots and some field trips didn't appear in the time table. JCU can help you with all of this upon arrival. They might even approve classes that overlap a bit, so I would definitely tell coming students to worry less about class registration. I highly recommend getting more classes approved from Copenhagen University than 7 classes due to the high risk of the classes overlapping. I wrote to the professors of the classes I was interested in, and they all responded sharing the outline for the semester, which was very helpful.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I chose 3 second year subjects and 1 third year subject. I did exchange on my fourth semester of my bachelors.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Much more field work - that was absolutely amazing.
Many more assignments. The workload was very different from class to class. In my marine chemistry subject I had to hand in many lab reports and I had two quizzes that I had to study for during the semester. You can see this in the subject outline if you request it in an email to the professors.
The professors are very down to earth and talkative. They all do very cool research and I felt more personally connected to them than the professors in Denmark. Especially because I went on 3 multi-day field trips.
The classes in general didn't have the academic level of reflection that I was used to at Copenhagen University. All my second year subjects were more focused on definitions, basic terms and understanding the science. The classes are less broad and more focused, which I liked.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
CH2042 Marine Chemistry
BZ3740 Wildlife Ecology and Management
BZ2725 Australian Terrestrial Diversity
EV2401 Australian landscape processes and evolution

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I absolutely loved my classes with Conrad 'Wildlife ecology and management' and 'Australian terrestrial diversity'. He is amazing and down to earth. You do wildlife surveys - learning to trap animals and ID them. The Australian nature is a great experience. When conrad was guiding you it felt very safe too. The field work in the two classes is very similar though. In 'Wildlife ecology and management' we spent 4 days in the outback doing wildlife surveys. That field trip was so unique.
Marine Chemistry had a big workload, but other than that I really liked the class. We went on a very cool field trip to Orpheus Island with magroves, black tipped reef sharks and stingrays, and that field trip in itself made the class worth it. I learned a lot in this class.

Field trips were quite expensive. I paid 3400 DKK for 3 multi-day field trips.
Visum: 3100 DKK
Students services and amenities (whatever that is): 750 DKK

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport: I bought a terrible used bike for 185 DKK. I took the bus sometimes. Student dayticket costs like $3.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
EVERYTHING! this is one of the best things about Australia - and a great way to make friends.
Both sports, academic, dive club, board games.
International café every tuesday with free coffee and snacks was a great and effortless way to connect with friends.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Social sports - where you can choose between different sports is a great way to meet new people. Your level of experience doesn't matter.
I got my Open water with the dive club on a liveaboard. This was a really good trip and I met a lot of my good friends on this trip. This way you also met people who wanted to go on dive trips later in the semester.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I visited Melbourne, and that was absolutely fantastic - the food, the culture, the music.
Go to Cairns! visit the Daintree rainforest, go diving on the GBR and see the beautiful waterfalls on the way there.
Visit Airlie beach and the whitsundays - here you can drive inland and see platypusses and broken river and drive to Cape Hillsborough national park at sunrise where kangaroos visit the beach.
Magnetic Island!! I was there four times.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Townsville is a bit of a redneck city where you encounter the people you imagine when you think of a real Australian with a mullet and a cowboy hat. The people in Townsville were so friendly and they want to hear about your culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Field trips and all the clubs are a good way to meet new students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The people who studied on the second year at uni that I had classes with were mostly 19 years old. I am 23, so that age difference sometimes made it difficult to bond. They are either very focused on drinking and think it is the best thing in the world or they don't really drink at all.
Many Australians haven't left the country.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The kindness, the interest in my country, the 'ohhh nowwwws', the welcoming to join them and their friends in going to a rugby game or the waterpark, the helpfullness, their relationship to nature - a lot of them really enjoy being outdoors and finding animals

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be patient - friendships take time.
Take advantage of the amazing nature that surrounds you.
JCU campus is great - enjoy the clubs, events and free food.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are free volleyball courts at George Roberts Hall and Rotary that you should definitely take advantage off.
Check in the subject outline what kind of exams the different subjects have. I ended up with four closed book exams and the workload in the exam period was immense...

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The adventure spirit shared by all the exchange students was my favorite thing.
Everyday people would spontaneously want to play volleyball, go salsa dancing at the Heritage Exchange and watch the sunset from the pontoons at Ross River. I spent so few weekends outside the exam period actually in Townsville, because I was going on trips almost every weekend in the beautiful surrounding nature - all you need is to rent a car.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I was surprised by how difficult it was to form deep connections to people, which at times felt lonely. It was difficult both due to the cultural differences, the fact that most Australians already have a network and many friends and the age differences. But also it takes a lot of effort and reaching out to form friendships. Be patient and happy with the friends you do make quite naturally through shared experiences - it is alright to seek some safety.
You are far away in Australia with a big time difference. I barely spoke to people at home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Just do it! I had the best time of my life.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
